changes.current_line: Billing that helps you grow revenue.
changes.change: For product and engineering buyers whose billing is homegrown: "Stop billing being a tax on the roadmap." Change a price, add a trial or set proration in a few clicks instead of waiting a quarter for engineering. Show the price-change demo early, since it drew the reaction: "that's a quarter of roadmap in five minutes."
changes.why: Owen explicitly rejected the revenue-growth framing in favor of "a tax on the roadmap," and the price-change demo was the part that landed.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: Offer a business-case session in the first or second meeting to build "a number that's ours": what the buyer's current billing system costs them, including slow pricing changes and subscriptions that lapse when a card fails and nobody chases it. Give the champion a short CFO-facing summary of that number. Keep the general study as backup, not the lead.
changes.why: Owen said "I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours" and was sent only the general ROI deck, so the payback case was never built before the freeze.

changes.change: Add a migration proof point for buyers moving off a homegrown billing system: move existing subscriptions over without asking customers for their card details again, cut over in stages, and plan around the buyer's busy season. Pair it with an offer to connect them with a reference customer who has migrated.
changes.why: Owen asked about moving subscriptions without re-collecting cards and about staged cutover, and the engineering lead said "we don't touch billing before renewal season."

changes.change: For finance-facing copy aimed at the approver, add a line that turns the roadmap problem into a cost already burning: a homegrown system with no owner means every pricing change takes a quarter, and failed-card lapses go unchased. Frame it as an ongoing cost, not an improvement, since "if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded."
changes.why: Finance saw the project as a "nice to have" and the funding bar reported was "if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded," so copy that speaks only to product pain would not clear it.
